method: Direct assistant translation of every normalized Arabic automatic-caption segment in two consecutive batches; no external translation service, audiovisual review or new independent reference verification. Speaker claims and qualifications preserved, with contextual repairs flagged.

segments.text: Peace be upon you. In this episode, we continue discussing
the most important fundamental questions about the world
of jinn: their origin, who their father is, why
they were created, whether some were created specifically to be devils
and that was their destiny, and what the qarin,
the companion, is. Was it created to be a companion? In
this episode we will discuss common misconceptions and ideas, some
of which we may even find in our scholarly heritage. This does not
necessarily mean that the scholars were wrong.
We must also understand that many
matters concerning jinn belong to the realm
of the unseen, about which most people
know only what revelation contains. Revelation
does not mention many of these details. So
many questions about this subject
draw on other accounts and sightings,
including Israelite traditions and accounts from unbelievers,
segments.review_notes: Israelite traditions and non-Muslim accounts are source categories in the presenter’s argument; do not infer that every such account is false or verified.

segments.text: from non-Muslims. Truth and falsehood became mixed. But
in our own age, we have gained access to other
cultures too, even cultures of polytheists,
and much has been translated for us that was not known
before.
Added to this are testimonies from people who may not
be Muslims, even atheists, about their sightings
of aliens and other things. As these accounts have multiplied,
they too have become far more numerous than what was known
before. We can add accounts from sorcerers
who bewitched people and then repented, who had contact
with the world of jinn and know more about it than others,
and from ruqyah practitioners discussing their experiences and what
they know of jinn, through Muslim jinn or
other jinn they interact with who are not
Muslim. When all these testimonies are translated
and reach us through the internet, it becomes possible
for a student of Islamic knowledge, even a young one,
provided they have the tools to examine, understand, and distinguish
truth from falsehood, to discover matters
segments.review_notes: Comparative claim that modern access can exceed early scholars’ available information is his methodological argument, not verification of online testimony.

segments.text: and details unavailable to the greatest imams in
history. Another point: we may disagree with some
statements of the great imams, but usually over
unimportant details that entail no practical action.
Usually, too, we favour one of the views
already known in the past. Rarely might
we put forward new ideas, suggestions, or interpretations,
but not on matters of religious law where
we would say we should not depart from the predecessors' positions.
Nor are these matters of creed; these too are issues that
segments.review_notes: Speaker distinguishes speculative details from creed/legal duties. This does not mean every claim later in the episode is outside theology.

segments.text: entail no practical action, so disagreement over them
is not important. Many of these matters
are not important to many people, which is why
revelation did not address them. But new developments,
doubts, and questions may now affect some people's faith,
so discussing them matters,
especially when we try to answer questions whose
answers people find in other religions,
the New Age movement, and other pagan traditions. So
we also need to discuss these matters and clarify some
difficulties. The foundation is the search for truth
and the attempt to build knowledge in a way pleasing to Allah,
glorified and exalted, not to enter into disputes
and conflicts. If any of you disagrees with us on an
idea, our starting point should be to seek
the truth and make allowances for one another. Let us not forget
the noble hadith: whoever learns knowledge to rival
segments.review_notes: Hadith paraphrase through the Arabic caption. Inherited Tirmidhi 2654 / Ibn Majah 253–254 locators and grading labels were not independently rechecked in this pass.

segments.text: scholars, argue with fools, or turn people's attention
toward himself,
Allah will admit him to Hell—we seek refuge in Allah. We ask
Allah for success and sincerity.
Let us begin with the origin of jinn. What is their origin? As we know,
[Clears throat.] It is agreed that they were created from
segments.review_notes: Non-speech cue retained. Marij min nar rendered smokeless flame of fire; Qur’an 55:15 is the inherited source lead.

segments.text: a smokeless flame of fire, as the noble verse states.
The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said in a hadith
in Sahih Muslim: the angels were created from light, the
jann from a smokeless flame of fire, and Adam from what has been described
to you—that is, earth, or light [uncertain caption wording]. So
segments.review_notes: Caption says earth or light. Retained with an uncertainty marker; do not silently turn نور into طين. Muslim 2996 and original audio require comparison.

segments.text: their origin is fire. But saying
they were created from fire does not mean that all jinn today
segments.review_notes: ASR omits a negation, but the following comparison with human bodies makes the intended sense does not mean clear. Contextual repair, audio pending.

segments.text: have the nature or appearance of fire,
because even our bodies do not resemble earth.
Our father was created from earth at the beginning, and then we
reproduce. There are contemporary interpretations that may not
be necessary; let us mention them briefly. I have found some
people attempting an explanation that perhaps
the body of a jinni is plasma,
segments.review_notes: Plasma is a proposed analogy mentioned by the presenter, not an independently established composition of jinn. Simplified ionization explanation also requires a separate scientific check.

segments.text: the fourth state of matter. Gas itself
may become ionized under enormous pressure or energy,
or intense heat, becoming ionized as atoms
and electrons separate.
This is not essential. But we understand that they have
bodies and souls, just as our bodies too
are inhabited by souls. Their bodies likewise come from
fire and contain souls. When a jinni dies,
its soul goes to the world of barzakh, as ours does.
segments.review_notes: Barzakh and bodily fate are theological claims; no independently inspected passage for each detail in this translation pass.

segments.text: There is also disagreement about what happens to its body.
Some scholars said it may be buried as
we are buried. Some accounts support this,
in books collecting many reports that may include plenty
of fanciful stories and legends, such as al-Hawatif by Ibn
segments.review_notes: Al-Hawatif is the spoken short title; inherited registry identifies Hawatif al-Jinan. Exact funeral accounts and chains remain to be reviewed.

segments.text: Abi al-Dunya,
which collected many accounts, including, for example,
people hearing jinn accompanying their dead
to burial. Even if these accounts are authentic,
a funeral procession does not necessarily mean it will be followed by
burial. These are accounts, and this is one view. Another view
is that when a jinni dies, its body, originally created from fire,
evaporates,
or dissolves away. I favour this view, and Allah knows
segments.review_notes: Body dissolution is explicitly his preferred view. Preserve Allah knows best and distinguish the alternative burial account.

segments.text: best. Here, however, we should not forget what we said
earlier in the Shasta episode, Mount Shasta: that they have
segments.review_notes: Mount Shasta reference, cities and other dimensions are the presenter’s account and model, not independently established geography or physics.

segments.text: cities, and their cities are built. So in their world,
which is in another dimension, there are buildings and
cities and things that may be tangible to them
but not to us.
So
their bodies may be tangible to them but not
to us. The point is to avoid the idea
that their bodies are transparent
and they live in our world,
and that, being transparent, they cannot
grasp things, and therefore cannot build
a civilization, cities, or houses, so they live in crevices
and holes, as many imagine. In
my view, this is a common misconception. They can
build. Some are like Bedouins, some live
among us, and some, the ‘awamir, for example, may live
segments.review_notes: ‘Awamir refers to inhabitants associated with homes. The alternate-dimensional-house explanation at 127–131 is explicitly conjectural.

segments.text: in our homes,
intruding upon us, and they may be Muslims.
Even the idea of ‘awamir, or inhabitants,
may have another meaning. They do not necessarily live in
our houses, but in houses of their own at the same location
as ours, in another dimension. All these ideas
may be right or wrong. Now we turn to the question of who
the father from whom they descend is, having finished discussing
their creation from fire. Even this idea
is disputed; these are all interpretations. Again,
these are questions with no practical action attached.
The most widespread view among our scholars
is that jinn are the children of Iblis, who is like Adam.
This was transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas, al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, and Qatadah,
and chosen by Shaykh al-Islam. The evidence is: will you take him
segments.review_notes: Shaykh al-Islam is retained as spoken; inherited source map identifies Ibn Taymiyyah. No new check of each early-authority attribution.

segments.text: and his offspring as allies instead of Me? I do not consider this
the stronger view, and Allah knows best. Others have said
so too. There are several responses; I will summarize them
in three points. First, yes, Iblis may have
offspring, but this does not mean that all jinn
segments.review_notes: ASR reverses the relation, literally all his descendants are the jinn. Contextually rendered not all jinn are his descendants, consistent with the stated argument; audio needed.

segments.text: are his offspring. That does not follow from the verse.
The verse is also an address to human beings:
will you take Iblis and his offspring as allies instead of Allah?
We know that some jinn are Muslims. If we say that
all Iblis's children are those allies—that is,
devils—then this is impossible. All
his offspring would become devils, whereas we know that some
jinn are Muslims. Third, if we understand
offspring in the verse to mean a bloodline, this may
segments.review_notes: Distinguish his possible inference about lineage from what the verse necessarily entails; the speaker himself says not necessarily.

segments.text: mean that devils can only be Iblis's children.
This may lead—not necessarily, of course—
to the conclusion that devils are only his
children, as though we were saying their conduct is predetermined.
Again, that meaning does not necessarily follow.
But one might infer here that devils
can only come from his lineage, even if
we say that not everyone in his lineage is a devil, but that devils
come only from his lineage. Even if this does not
make them compelled rather than free to choose, it still imposes
a restriction: that devils can only come from
his lineage. So I think, and Allah knows best, that to understand
the verse we should return to its beginning: when We told the angels
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 18:50 paraphrase. The pre-existing-species inference and subsequent fairness argument are the presenter’s interpretation, not additional verse wording.

segments.text: to prostrate before Adam, they prostrated except Iblis; he was of the jinn
and disobeyed his Lord's command. Will you then take him and his offspring...?
He was of the jinn, in the past tense: he belonged to a kind
already in existence, the jinn. He was selected to attend
this gathering and be charged with prostrating, like
the angels. I ask here, and Allah knows best: is it reasonable
that humans and jinn are both morally responsible kinds, yet
humans are the children of an honoured prophet, Adam,
while the other kind are the children of Satan? Even
if we say Iblis was obedient and then disobeyed
at this gathering, that is a possibility, not a certainty.
They were his children when he was obedient, and then he disobeyed
later. Even here, you may find—
I do not say a logical impossibility, but something reason finds
hard to accept—that all morally responsible jinn are the children
of a defiant devil, rebellious against Allah,
glorified and exalted, the head of evil in existence
among humans and jinn. I say here, and Allah knows best, perhaps
what occurred to our great scholars who
segments.review_notes: ASR ما خطر can be read as negation or a relative construction in this fragment. Rendered what occurred to the scholars to fit the following proposal; audio check required.

segments.text: held this view was that the story of jinn and humans
began together, and then one was chosen to prostrate
before the other. Even so, I find this difficult to accept.
If we ourselves were among the jinn, we would
ask why our father was ordered to prostrate before their father.
There is a difficulty. Again, I do not say this
contradicts reason and self-evident truths,
but
I find a problem with it. When both kinds are morally responsible,
the starting point is that they should be equal in responsibility
and honour, at least, so that the ancestor
of one kind is not asked to prostrate before the ancestor of the other,
even if they differ in other characteristics. Allah
knows best. So the stronger view, in my opinion, and Allah knows best—
again, this disagreement is not a serious matter—is that Iblis
belongs to an ancient kind that already existed,
and is not their father. He is the son of one of them. Perhaps their father
existed thousands of years earlier. Some accounts even
say that jinn existed two thousand years before Adam.
segments.review_notes: Two-thousand-year chronology is an attributed report, not a confirmed date. Other jinn attending/prostrating and Iblis already being rebellious are hypotheses.

segments.text: Then Iblis was asked to attend. Perhaps other jinn,
leaders among them, attended this gathering and prostrated,
and only Iblis rebelled. Nor do I rule out
that Iblis himself had already been rebellious
beforehand,
and was not brought there because he was honoured, as the accounts say.
I believe all these are Israelite traditions. Perhaps Iblis
segments.review_notes: Speculation that Iblis supplied stories to people altering scripture is the presenter’s unverified account, not established textual history.

segments.text: himself even passed these fanciful stories
to those who altered the Torah,
to diminish the gravity of his sin. He was not necessarily
obedient and then, at that moment, suddenly became
a rebellious, arrogant devil. Especially since we also have
accounts saying that jinn were on earth,
disobeyed, and were replaced. Some scholars of
tafsir said: jinn were created before Adam, peace be upon him,
and before them on earth were the hinn and binn.
segments.review_notes: Hinn and binn names and pre-Adamic history are explicitly uncertain at 223–224. Do not upgrade them because inherited registry labels say verified.

segments.text: Allah gave the jinn power over them; they fought them, drove them
out, removed them, and settled there, and so on.
Allah knows best. These are all accounts whose truth
we do not know, and there is no evidence. Perhaps we could say
they were punished through another successor: the appearance of humanity.
Iblis's attendance was to witness this event, the existence of
the successor whose kind would give rise to humans who would
succeed them on this earth.
Perhaps he too was a leader of the wicked
among jinn, and came not to be honoured but to witness
this event.
His attendance was a punishment or humiliation,
not an honour. So in my view, the stronger interpretation
of the verse, will you take him and his offspring, is that “offspring”
segments.review_notes: Offspring as helpers is a proposed interpretive view. It should not replace the literal reading without attribution or a checked tafsir passage.

segments.text: here, as scholars holding the other view said,
means his helpers among the jinn, not his children. Even
so, we do not say anything prevents Iblis himself having
wives, not just one wife, and descendants and children.
But his own children too are not destined to be
devils. Otherwise, they would be compelled, not
free to choose. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn ‘Abbas:
segments.review_notes: Al-Dahhak / Ibn ‘Abbas report about Iblis’s children and lifespan; the presenter questions attribution. Original chain/grading not checked here.

segments.text: the devils are Iblis's children and do not die except with
Iblis.
This even conflicts with the other account,
or at least partly conflicts with the idea that Iblis
is the father of all jinn, also narrated from Ibn
‘Abbas. All these accounts are transmitted without
a chain of transmission,
and their attribution to Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him,
segments.review_notes: Sentence continues through the prayer at 250. English places the uncertainty predicate at 250 for readable continuity, without adding a claim.

segments.text: is uncertain.
But we also cannot rule out that Iblis had
other devils with him, of lesser rank,
who were granted respite as he was, to remain until
the end of time. They need not, however, be
his children. The second view, also narrated from
Ibn ‘Abbas, is that the father of jinn is not Iblis but someone
else called Suma or Sumiya. You now find many
segments.review_notes: Suma/Sumiya are provisional transliterations of سوما / سوميا, not securely established names of a real ancestor. Speaker cautions against invented details.

segments.text: rumours, and even YouTube channels publishing
numerous details about him. We know nothing about him
that would allow us to discuss such details. Perhaps
all of this comes from Israelite traditions. Some also said
the father of jinn is called al-Jann, because the verse says:
And the jann We created before, from scorching fire.
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 15:27 and 55:15 allusions; interpreting al-jann as an ancestor’s proper name is distinct from the verses themselves.

segments.text: And in Surat al-Rahman: He created the jann from a smokeless flame
of fire. They said al-jann appears here in the singular,
as an ancestor, so perhaps it is the father's name. Here,
though, I suggest a third view, which may be mistaken.
segments.review_notes: Multiple ancestors is explicitly a proposal that may be mistaken; retain that qualification.

segments.text: Again, interpretation here is not a grave matter. They may
have several ancestors. Why? Because they belong to
numerous, very different kinds. Here we recall
the authentic hadith: jinn are of three kinds—one kind has
segments.review_notes: Three-kinds hadith rendered from caption. Authenticity is the speaker’s attribution; inherited primary locator and grading still require audit.

segments.text: wings and flies in the air, one consists of snakes and dogs,
and one settles and travels. We will explain this
in another episode about their kinds. But
they appear to be numerous and very different kinds.
We will also come to some scholars' statement that
the differences between them resemble the differences between animals,
segments.review_notes: Ant/elephant comparison attributed to unnamed scholars. No exact author or original passage supplied here.

segments.text: from an ant to an elephant. This is what I favour, and what
also appears from newer accounts
and sightings of aliens and others. The stronger possibility, Allah
knows best, is that they also have different ancestors. Perhaps
our scholars interpreted this hadith as meaning
that the differences between these kinds are not great:
they differ, but all descend from one father.
Ultimately, neither we nor they know the details,
and disagreement on this point is not very serious.
Now we turn to a very important matter, more important than
everything before it: jinn are morally responsible. The fundamental
purpose of their creation is worship: I created
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 51:56 paraphrase; repeated later. Translation does not import wording from a named modern English edition.

segments.text: jinn and humans only to worship Me. Allah also says,
reporting their words in Surat al-Jinn: among us
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 72:11 and 72:14 paraphrases; Ibn al-Qayyim’s three-rank description at 294–297 is a separate source claim.

segments.text: are the righteous and those otherwise; we follow different paths.
And in the same surah: among us are those who submit
and those who deviate. Ibn al-Qayyim therefore said:
they fall into three ranks, like humans—the righteous, those below
the righteous, and unbelievers—just as humans include the devout,
those taking a middle course, meaning Muslims of an intermediate rank, and unbelievers.
Unfortunately, in my view, you find a rare and anomalous
opinion, but one that does exist: that some among them, the devils,
were created that way, as angels were. Angels
were created without such moral testing and do not disobey Allah's
segments.review_notes: Without taklif rendered without such moral testing in this comparison. Avoid implying angels have no divine commands or duties.

segments.text: commands; so some devils too were created to be
devils. This cannot be right. The principle is: I created
jinn and humans only to worship Me. A devil
chose disbelief and chose to become a devil.
We find this view, this anomalous view,
for example, in a book by Shaykh ‘Ali
al-Tantawi, may Allah have mercy on him, called A General Introduction
segments.review_notes: A General Introduction to Islam is a descriptive title translation for al-Tantawi’s book. The claimed error needs comparison with the exact edition and passage.

segments.text: to Islam. Although he wrote it to introduce people,
non-Muslims, to Islam, it contains this
mistake. This, of course, does not negate his learning,
or that of others who held this view. But I believe
this is a genuinely serious idea, and I suspect
it also reached us from the altered Torah and Jewish-Christian
segments.review_notes: Claim of Jewish-Christian influence is an unverified historical inference; neither doctrine nor popular culture is uniform across those traditions.

segments.text: culture.
As we have mentioned more than once, they
do not have something called jinn. They have
angels in this unseen world, some of whom became
devils, fallen angels: Iblis
and his company. They also believe—and this is a serious idea
you find in Hollywood films,
games, and popular culture—
that these devils, originally angels,
are the kings of Hell. Hell is the kingdom
in the underworld, and its kings
are these beings. This closely resembles the angels of punishment
in Islam and in revelation since Adam's time.
The angels of punishment too were created with a fearsome appearance,
segments.review_notes: Fearsome appearance and lack of feeling in angels are presenter claims; no direct scriptural citation for those details is supplied here.

segments.text: created to punish people, but they themselves,
although present in Hell, are not punished.
Their task is punishment and inflicting punishment, but they do not
suffer it. They were created without feeling, and their task
is to carry out these commands, Allah's commands.
You find the same idea in that culture:
Satan and his company, although they disobeyed Allah,
glorified and exalted, have the role in Hell of being
its kings. They delight in this power,
delight in misleading people, and bring them
into their world to punish them, not to suffer punishment themselves.
This is a very serious idea. We find it in several
films; I will mention only two examples. One film is called
Little Nicky, a Hollywood film released in
2000, starring Adam Sandler. Briefly, its story is that
Satan, meaning Iblis himself, becomes involved in
segments.review_notes: Identifying a fictional Satan with Islamic Iblis is the presenter’s framing; the film is not religious evidence.

segments.text: a conflict with his three sons. The eldest
and youngest enter a conflict with their father,
segments.review_notes: Eldest and youngest retained as captioned; the next lines separately call Nicky the youngest. This internal inconsistency needs original audio/film-synopsis comparison.

segments.text: disagreeing with him over power. They go out
into the world, specifically to New York,
and come into conflict with humans. They rebel. Then
the youngest son, Nicky, who is kind,
simple, and clumsy, wants to follow them
and bring them back. He becomes involved in comic events
and, as always in Hollywood, a love story with
a human girl like us in New York, and so
the story goes. It wants us to sympathize with him
in the end. He is perfectly normal, but he descends
from these jinn,
these devils. The idea is that some
devils may return to their angelic origin,
while retaining a devil's appearance:
red, with horns, long ears, a tail, and so on.
Another famous character is Hellboy. He began
in comic books in 1993, and films based on them
segments.review_notes: Hellboy debut year and mixed comic/film plot remain the speaker’s summary; no new original comic or film inspection.

segments.text: are still being released, very well known.
Briefly, the story is that toward the end of the Second
World War, the Nazis, or a Russian sorcerer,
wanted to open a gateway to Hell
and obtain a weapon from it.
But the plan failed. The gateway opened for seconds,
and in those seconds a baby came through,
an infant,
a little devil: Hellboy,
meaning the son or child of Hell. His father was one
of Hell's kings, a powerful devil,
and his mother a witch. So he is half human and half devil.
A British scientist discovers him
and raises him, so he grows up like us. He looks like a devil but is
kind like us.
He also has extraordinary powers, being a devil or
half devil, and helps people. We also have here
a very weak hadith that I think is
segments.review_notes: Very weak report is distinguished from the earlier three-kinds report. Exact grading/number and comparison require original hadith-source audit.

segments.text: problematic: Allah created jinn in three kinds,
one consisting of snakes and scorpions, one like the wind in the air,
and one subject to reckoning and punishment. Another version
says a third are like the children of Adam. Even from its
style, it is clear this is not the Prophet's speech, peace and blessings
be upon him. It conflicts with the verse: I created jinn
and humans only to worship Me. It is not that one third
were created as devils and are subject to reckoning and punishment.
segments.review_notes: Speaker’s devils gloss is not identical to the report’s wording about accountability. Preserve the distinction when adapting this argument.

segments.text: All are morally responsible. Al-Albani therefore classified this hadith
in his series of weak
and fabricated hadiths. It conflicts with the authentic hadith
we mentioned earlier: they are three kinds,
one with wings, one consisting of snakes and scorpions—or, in a version, dogs—
segments.review_notes: Snakes and scorpions, then or dogs, retained from caption. Compare original audio and report wording; do not silently unify the two narrations.

segments.text: and one that settles and travels. All are morally responsible. Also,
let us not forget this point: if we say a devil
was created as a devil, then it should not be punished.
The verses clearly say it is punished. Allah said
to Iblis: the truth—and the truth I speak—is that I will fill Hell
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 38:84–85 paraphrase. No modern translator’s verbatim wording copied.

segments.text: with you and all those among them who follow you,
meaning humans and jinn. An even clearer verse describes Iblis
entering the Fire: Satan says, when the matter is decided,
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 14:22 paraphrase; the concluding we will all be punished is the speaker’s explanation, not presented as an additional ayah.

segments.text: Allah made you a true promise; I promised you and failed you.
I had no authority over you except that I called you
and you answered me. Do not blame me; blame yourselves.
I cannot come to your rescue, nor you to mine.
That means neither I will help you nor you help me. We will all
be punished. These are Iblis's words. So Iblis himself
will be punished, and everyone who follows him among the devils
will be punished. They also said that, linguistically, “shaytan”
means any arrogant rebel, from shatan,
segments.review_notes: Arabic etymological explanation is the speaker’s account; exact lexicon definitions and alternative derivations require checking.

segments.text: meaning extreme rebellion.
That is why “shaytan” also describes human devils,
as the verse says: thus We appointed for every prophet
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 6:112 allusion supports the description of human and jinn devils; it does not independently settle the etymology of Iblis.

segments.text: an enemy, devils among humans and jinn. “Shaytan” is a description,
a title applied to Iblis. His name was Iblis;
when he rebelled and disbelieved, he became a devil. Some
scholars, unfortunately, went to great lengths to find
an Arabic meaning for the word “Iblis.” It is his name,
not because he despaired of Allah's mercy,
or lost hope in it. That is one view,
but the stronger view is that this is his real name. Even
al-‘Aqqad, in his book Iblis, said that he found
segments.review_notes: Al-‘Aqqad’s Iblis is the named linguistic source. Claimed cross-language occurrence and proposed original name require the book passage, not broad inference.

segments.text: the word Iblis in all, or many,
earlier languages and religions, because that is
his real name. Allah knows best. Even if there are
accounts saying his earlier name was ‘Azazil, for example,
or Baal, or something else, the stronger view is that his real name
is the one given in the Qur’an. We conclude this
section by saying that Iblis and all devils chose
disbelief and disobedience; they were not created that way.
Even so, although there are human devils,
Iblis remains the head of evil in
both worlds. Why? Because he is the oldest. He
existed before Adam, before devils emerged
from Adam's lineage: human devils. Also, Iblis
rebelled against Allah, glorified and exalted, in
His presence.
This is something no one would dare do. Indeed,
Allah, glorified, speaks to no human except
segments.review_notes: Universal claim about divine speech is translated as speaker wording; its scope needs a separate theological source check.

segments.text: the prophets. But Iblis
had this opportunity and rebelled against Allah,
glorified and exalted, before the angels, addressing Him with this rebellion
and arrogance. Add to this that Iblis
existed before all of us and will remain until the end.
He is the leader of evil throughout this story, from its beginning
to its end. Even if some human devils
rival Iblis, their influence,
however far it reaches into later generations, remains limited
in time and place and to particular peoples; it does not extend
to every other people. Iblis himself, however,
is the king of evil in both worlds, human
and jinn. His lifespan extends beyond that of all
human beings. He is also the only one who plays the role
of a god. All the false gods
segments.review_notes: Identifying all false gods or chief evil gods with Iblis is the presenter’s comparative-religion theory, not an established historical identity.

segments.text: worshipped in other religions,
as we have mentioned in several episodes,
particularly the chief of the evil gods, turn out
to be Iblis himself. He is the one worshipped among all peoples
who disbelieved, unlike Pharaoh or other human beings
who claimed divinity and were worshipped only in a limited
time and place.
Now we turn to the qarin,
continuing the previous question. The companion is established in
the Qur’an: his companion says, here is what I have ready;
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 50:23 and 50:27 use companion in different contexts. Do not assume both refer to the same kind of companion; tafsir must distinguish the recording/presenting angel from the misleading companion.

segments.text: his companion says, our Lord, I did not cause him to transgress. We also have,
in Surat al-Zukhruf: whoever turns away from remembrance of the Most Merciful,
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 43:36 allusion; assignment versus compulsion is the presenter’s subsequent theological explanation.

segments.text: We assign him a devil who becomes his companion. This companion is also
a jinni who chose disbelief and chose to dominate a person,
perhaps spending its life misleading humans.
Since, in our estimation, jinn are very
numerous, those who went astray among them,
the devils, may even outnumber human beings.
segments.review_notes: Population estimates and proposed competition/motives among companions are conjectures, not quantified observations.

segments.text: So
you could find a devil imposing itself on every person.
Perhaps they compete to toy with us.
The question is: why? Why attach itself to us?
First, perhaps for amusement, to amuse itself by toying with us,
as human devils do. There is also the desire for power:
seeing you disbelieve because of it, taking pleasure in controlling
a person, especially when we cannot see it.
It also intrudes on the person it accompanies,
sharing their food and drink, and sometimes even
segments.review_notes: Food, drink, sexual intrusion and watching a person are speaker claims; no diagnosis, individual threat assessment or practical treatment advice follows from them.

segments.text: their wife if they do not seek refuge in Allah.
It may become a lover, falling in love with the person. We
will discuss this in a separate episode, Allah willing.
It amuses itself by watching the person naked or in the bathroom.
It may also seek to please those stronger than itself,
the powerful devils, up to Iblis. I believe, then,
that the qarin is one of the lesser jinn, not the great ones,
segments.review_notes: Rank, size and abilities of ordinary companions versus rulers’ companions are explicitly his estimate.

segments.text: unless it is
the companion of a human king or one of the great
human devils, in which case it may be one of the powerful
rebels. But for an ordinary person, I imagine,
in my estimation, the devil accompanying them is small in form,
ability, and size. Another important
point: it does not stay with us in every circumstance. When
segments.review_notes: Claims about when a companion withdraws are not independently checked here. Do not treat an individual experience as proof of the companion’s presence or absence.

segments.text: we seek refuge in Allah,
when we are in a spiritual state, the normal expectation is that it does not
come near us. Even when we pray, when we say it
whispers to us, if we seek refuge in Allah, it retreats and withdraws.
It is not with us in every circumstance,
particularly when a Muslim enters the bathroom
and seeks refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. The normal expectation
is that it is not with them then either.
Here we come to a noble hadith in Muslim: none
segments.review_notes: Muslim 2814a is the inherited lead for the assigned-companion report, and 2815 for ‘A’ishah’s report. No new original-source check in this pass.

segments.text: of you is without an assigned companion from among the jinn.
They asked: even you, Messenger of Allah? He said: even me. Also,
in ‘A’ishah's hadith, when she became jealous concerning him, he said:
has your devil come to you? She said: Messenger of Allah, do I have a devil?
He said yes. She asked: and does every person? He said
yes.
And you, Messenger of Allah? And so the hadith continues. Perhaps
this is where Shaykh al-Tantawi and others got their view:
that every person has one assigned to them.
The verse also says We assign him one. Perhaps they inferred
segments.review_notes: ASR نقيد contextually repaired to نقيض from the earlier verse and argument; audio pending.

segments.text: that every person has a devil, and so the devil
was, as it were, created to be a devil. But we return
to the principle: I created jinn and humans only
to worship Me. The jinni freely chose to become
a devil, and was assigned. This assignment is not compulsion
from Allah. Allah, glorified and exalted, gave it this
opportunity, and it imposed itself on us. We infer this
from other verses too. Allah says concerning unbelievers:
had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you.
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 4:90 allusion; permission/compulsion analogy is the presenter’s argument, not a new translation of the entire verse.

segments.text: That is, He chose to give unbelievers power; He did not tell them:
disbelieve and dominate.
He enabled them. Also: had Allah willed,
He would have overcome them Himself, but He tests some of you through others.
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 47:4 allusion. Garbled يبلون الله بالكفار at 530 contextually rendered Allah tests us through unbelievers; confirm audio.

segments.text: Allah tests us through unbelievers. Allah, glorified, did not order
unbelievers to disbelieve. They chose disbelief,
chose to fight Islam, and refused
to accept its call, moving on to fight
Muslims. Likewise, an unbelieving jinni
chose disbelief. Allah, glorified, allowed
it to impose itself on us; He did not command it
to do so. Further evidence is that
the companion itself will disown us. The verse says:
his companion says, our Lord, I did not cause him to transgress; he was already
segments.review_notes: Qur’an 50:27 allusion; responsibility argument and comparison with angels are the presenter’s explanation.

segments.text: far astray. It disowns him and is punished. If it were simply
doing its job as an angel does,
and an angel is not called to account, then the jinni would not be called to account,
or this devilish companion should not be punished.
The decisive evidence with which we conclude this point
is also that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was able
to influence the companion assigned to him,
and it accepted Islam. Nothing prevents the possibility
segments.review_notes: Fa-aslama / fa-aslamu has a known interpretive/vocalization issue requiring the original hadith commentary. The translation preserves his chosen accepted Islam reading without presenting it as the only reading.

segments.text: that a companion attached to one of us might also become Muslim simply through
accompanying us and hearing the Qur’an. Perhaps it becomes Muslim
and leaves us, and another companion, another devil, comes
segments.review_notes: Replacement, death and succession of companions are speculative scenarios, not established by the cited hadith merely by analogy.

segments.text: and attaches itself to us. So we should not take “companion”
to mean this being has been set over us
irrevocably, inevitably, and forever. It may even die before
we do, and another comes and imposes itself on us.
We may also die while the companion remains alive,
and it imposes itself on another person, and so on. It is simply
a trial for us; Allah tests us through them. Perhaps there is also
a jinn companion accompanying another jinni.
segments.review_notes: A jinni having another jinni as a companion is expressly hypothetical.

segments.text: In their world too, there may be whispering
and trials, because they too are morally responsible. What matters
in this discussion is that they are morally responsible
like us, and impose themselves on us only by their own choice.
Perhaps one repents and Allah accepts its repentance. Here
other questions arise: are we better than them? Do
they have prophets and messengers? And further questions:
what are their characteristics and appearances? We will devote
other episodes to all this, Allah willing. I hope
you have benefited from this episode. If you have found it
beneficial, try sharing it so that the benefit
segments.review_notes: Invitation to share is the original speaker’s closing request, not an instruction to tools or future agents.

segments.text: spreads. We seek refuge in Allah from [incomplete phrase] the accursed. We ask
segments.review_notes: ASR repeats من and omits the noun before accursed. Explicit incomplete-phrase marker preserves uncertainty rather than silently supplying Satan.

segments.text: Allah to help us against our devils and admit us
to Paradise together. Thank you for listening, and goodbye.
